title: What the Semantic Locator is
description: The locator answers 'where is this concept, in any language, any format, any field?' It takes a concept expressed one way — a word, a formula, a diagram label — and finds its counterparts elsewhere, with evidence for each match. It is the tool that stops the same idea from being reinvented in every discipline under a different name.

title: Cross-scale concept data model
description: A concept is a record with expressions at multiple rungs: colloquial terms, trade jargon, scientific terms, formal definitions, formulas, and diagram labels, each tagged with language and discipline. Bridges between rungs carry evidence — a dictionary entry, a paper's definition section, a standards document — so matches are checkable.

title: Hybrid matching algorithm
description: Matching combines two independent signals: embedding similarity across languages and symbolic checks like shared formulas, shared units, or shared definition structure. Either signal alone makes mistakes — embeddings confuse related-but-different concepts, symbols miss paraphrases — but their agreement is strong evidence of a true match.

demo.title: Runnable code demo — Hybrid matching algorithm

architecture: Dual-scorer architecture; embedding scorer over multilingual vectors; symbolic scorer over formulas, units, and definition overlap; agreement gate requiring both above threshold.

title: Abstraction-ladder traversal algorithm
description: A street term and a formal definition rarely match directly; the ladder climbs rung by rung, each step evidenced. 'Heat flow' matches the trade term 'thermal load', which matches the scientific 'heat transfer rate', which matches the formal 'dQ/dt'. Each rung's bridge is checked independently, so a weak link is visible instead of hidden.

title: Locate query interface specification
description: Callers submit an expression with its language, discipline, and abstraction rung, plus how much evidence they need. Responses list matching concepts with per-match evidence: which bridges fired, their strengths, and any disagreements. The interface never returns a bare match — evidence rides along or the match does not ship.

title: Ingestion: harvesting expressions and bridges
description: Expressions come from dictionaries, glossaries, standards, textbooks, and field interviews; bridges come from definition sections, translation memories, and bilingual experts. Ingestion normalizes each into rung-tagged expressions with source provenance, and never invents a bridge — unattested links stay absent, not guessed.

title: Reasoning: adjudicating conflicting matches
description: Two bridges can disagree — one source says term A means concept X, another says it means concept Y. The locator adjudicates with evidence strength, source reliability, and context: the same term can legitimately mean different things in different disciplines, and the locator says so instead of picking a false winner.

title: Failure modes: false friends and drift
description: Languages have false friends — same word, different concepts — and meanings drift over time. The locator defends with discipline scoping, temporal tagging of expressions, and symbolic checks that catch embedding mistakes. Suspected false-friend collisions are flagged, never silently merged.

title: Security: protecting linguistic communities
description: Expressions harvested from communities — especially indigenous and minority languages — carry rights. The locator records consent and usage terms per source, enforces them at query time, and never exposes restricted expressions. Communities can audit exactly how their language data was used.
